questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Since I had already been to the UK for my BA, I got a taste of how enriching a study exchange can be. I wanted to go somewhere very different from both my home (Denmark) and the UK. I have gotten increasingly interested in Korean culture, and this interest was the main reason why I chose South Korea. I chose Seoul and Sungkyunkwan University because of the history of the university, the accessability of the city, and the academics.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is quite possibly the best experience of my university history. I am deducting one point for the slight COVID-annoyances and troubles with paperwork, but despite these I never once regretted studying abroad or choosing my university.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Somewhat easy. I arrived at Incheon airport where several assistants from the different universities stood and guided the different arriving students where to go.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Help with quarantine-measures and taxi-service from airport to quarantine facility.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found it fairly easy, because I got my housing through an institution advertised by the university (HireVisa).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I would say it is definitely preferred to live off-campus. Most of the university housing in Seoul has curfew and requires you to live with a roommate. I was personally not in the mood for that. Off campus housing provides a lot of flexibility, and if you live near a subway station, it is fairly easy to get to campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very satisfied with the room I got. But for my building, you either got lucky like me and got a great room, or you could end up in a smaller room with a window facing a brick wall.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is very hectic, chaotic, and busy doing the registration at SKKU (and, I believe, most South Korean universities).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It's first come first serve, so you have to be quick to sign up for the classes you want. The university didn't send me my login information in time, so I got none of the classes I initially wanted. But there is another registration period afterwards where you can ask for a place in a class or sign up for exchange-specific classes. So I still got some interesting classes regardless.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was a (slightly) confusing guide on how to register, and then you had the option of mailing the university staff, though they were very overworked.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: As mentioned I got none of those I initially wanted. But it was super easy to register for exchange-only classes, and I got into another class fairly easy by asking the professor.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have a prepared list of classes beforehand. Also, be prepared to send kind emails to professors asking for a place in their classes in case you don't get them initially.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic level is lower than what I am used to, but the courses were super interesting!

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took courses which allowed both BA and MA students, so the academic level felt lower than what I am used to.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much more lecture style, where the professor talks and you write notes. For one of my classes there were no student discussions at all, which also was in part due to COVID-restrictions and us having the class entirely online and through pre-recorded sessions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
IEC4008: Understanding Asian Cultures.
IEC4009: Contemporary Korean Society and Culture.
SOC4010: Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: SOC4010: Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights. It was definitely the most engaging of my courses with loads of discussions on how AI impacts society. It also had a mix of students from both social science and computer science, which I believe made the discussions more diverse and interesting.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not necessarily unexpected, but you have to pay national health insurance (NHIS) once you get your ARC (alien registration card). And the bill turned out to be more than expected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I was told food is less expensive than at home, and that is absolutely correct! Public transportation is also super cheap.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think COVID prevented these from happening, but I also didn't seek them out, so I can't answer with certainty.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Same answer as above.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: They did arrange a hike for exchange students in smaller groups to comply with restrictions. I didn't go personally, but heard about it from other people, and it seemed like a great way to get to meet other exchange students.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: If you can, get out of the city and explore the rest of the country. It is incredibly diverse in nature and cityscapes. I can absolutely recommend Busan and Jeju Island, which are some of the biggest destinations.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I had tried to prepare myself mentally before leaving home, and because I had already had a slight introduction to the culture, it did not seem like too drastic a shift. That being said, it was very different.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Take advantage of your university assigned guide. And engage with those in your classes. Koreans are super nice but somewhat shy.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: For me it was mainly the food. More specifically the bread.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: They are very big on coffee and cafes. Eating out, especially if you're eating Korean food, is a very social thing.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Double-check all of you documents. 2) Connect with other UCPH students before going, so you have someone to compare/ask advice. 3) Visit the Suwon campus, even if you're studying at the Seoul campus. Also, bonus: try and get some coffee at the university library - there's a robot serving it!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university had a KakaoTalk group chat, which was super helpful since not only university staff could respond, but also other students, which was sometimes a lot quicker than sending the university an email.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing and living in a different culture, and especially experiencing it with other people who also were new to the country.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I would say COVID restrictions, but also the bread situation. Bread as a meal or culinary concept is very different in South Korea compared to Denmark and majority of Europe.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
